newsitem.title: UK: UK Conservative leadership challengers slug it out.
newsitem.headline: UK Conservative leadership challengers slug it out.

text.p: The five candidates for the leadership of Britain's battered Conservative party staged last-minute drives to win support on Monday, fighting to avoid being left out of the running in the first round.
The 164 Conservative members of parliament who survived Labour's May 1 election landslide vote on Tuesday for the man to face up to the new prime minister, Tony Blair.
Campaign teams were canvassing undeclared MPs and all five rivals have arranged cocktail parties near parliament on Monday evening to woo anyone who has not made up their mind.

Former Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke, a feisty, no-nonsense politician who fought a rearguard battle from within the cabinet against Major's rightward drift before the election, remains favourite to win the first round of the contest.
Several newspaper commentators see Clarke as the only Conservative able to stand up to Blair, already the most popular prime minister on record with an approval rating of 82 percent.
But the complex rules of the contest to replace former prime minister John Major as party -- and now opposition -- leader mean he is not certain of final victory.
To win outright, Clarke would have to secure more than half the vote and be 15 percent ahead of the runner-up. But Sunday newspapers put his support at around 35 MPs -- well short.
That leaves the door open for former Welsh secretary William Hague, at 36 by far the youngest in the field and tipped to come second in Tuesday's poll, to mount a strong challenge.

British newspapers said on Monday that the three remaining candidates: former interior minister Michael Howard, former social security secretary Peter Lilley and former cabinet minister John Redwood, were planning a pact to halt Clarke.
Under the pact only the strongest of the three -- all on the party's right -- would fight the second round to stop victory going to Clarke on the centre-left or Hague on the centre-right.
This means the contest, and the vote trading, will only start in earnest after the first ballot, the result of which is expected to be known at 1630 GMT on Tuesday.

For the second ballot on June 17, the winner needs more than 50 percent of the vote -- a tough task if there are more than two candidates. To complicate matters, new contenders can join the race for the second ballot.
If there is no outright victor on June 17 the two who top the poll will slug it out in a final ballot on June 19.

The contest has been criticised by grass-roots activists who say allowing only MPs to vote for the party leadership is undemocratic. But despite protests, the party leadership decided the rules could not be changed in time.
